extensions: Before building any model, conduct a consent audit: map every data point collected against the privacy policy and terms of service in effect at the time of collection, and segment the dataset into permitted, ambiguous, and prohibited buckets. Only the first bucket should be used in any model training.

Rather than training a general-purpose AI product for open sale, test the hypothesis with a single named pilot buyer under a bilateral data-sharing agreement — they get early model access, you get revenue and a reference customer.

Reframe the revenue model from selling a trained model to selling ongoing inference access via API — this keeps training data and weights proprietary, prevents buyers from extracting underlying customer behaviour patterns, and creates recurring revenue.
nonObviousAngles: The constraint baked into this framing is 'use the data we already have.' Removing that constraint opens a cleaner path: design an explicit data-contribution programme where customers opt in to share anonymised usage data in exchange for a benefit. This produces a smaller but legally clean dataset and turns customers into stakeholders.

The person most opposed to this idea — a privacy regulator or customer who reads the fine print — gets something important right: the value of the AI product is inseparable from the trust customers placed in the original service. If customers learn their private data was sold to third parties, reputational damage to the core business will likely exceed the revenue generated.

weaknesses.text: The legal basis for training on this data almost certainly does not exist. GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis for each processing purpose; using data for a new commercial purpose (training a model sold externally) is a distinct processing activity requiring its own basis. CCPA similarly prohibits selling personal information collected under a service relationship without opt-in consent where the secondary use is materially different. Proceeding exposes the company to regulatory enforcement, class-action exposure, and mandatory data deletion orders that would destroy the trained model itself.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The idea has no validated buyer. AI model buyers do not purchase generic behavioural models — they buy solutions to named problems with measurable ROI. The company does not know what problem the model solves for a buyer, whether the model's training domain matches any buyer's use case, or whether buyers would trust a model trained on another company's customer data. Committing engineering and data infrastructure before a named buyer commits to a pilot means building for an imaginary customer.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: Customers have an implicit trust contract this idea breaks. Even if legal consent is technically achievable through policy re-papering, customers who discover their private usage data was sold in model form to competitors or unrelated industries will experience this as betrayal. The backlash to similar moves by consumer platforms (LinkedIn's data scraping for AI training, Zoom's 2023 policy change) generated churn, regulatory scrutiny, and reputational damage disproportionate to the commercial gain.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The company's ML and data engineering capability to build a production AI product is assumed, not verified. Operating a sold inference product requires model versioning, SLA guarantees, security isolation between buyer sessions, monitoring for model drift, retraining pipelines, and a support function for buyer integration failures. These are capabilities of an AI platform company, not a SaaS company with usage data.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

weaknesses.text: The opportunity cost is unexamined. Building a standalone AI product is a company-defining strategic pivot, not a revenue line extension. Engineering, legal, data, and commercial resources will be drawn from the core product. The idea is presented as additive revenue but the execution cost means it functions as a strategic reallocation.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

risks: A regulatory investigation or data subject access request surfaces the training data pipeline before the product ships — resulting in mandatory halt, model deletion, and public disclosure that damages reputation with the existing customer base before earning any third-party revenue.
The first pilot buyer's legal due diligence rejects the data provenance, causing the pilot to collapse publicly and poisoning the category for future buyers.
A competitor or existing AI vendor already has a model trained on larger datasets with established buyer trust, making the company's offering non-competitive on day one.
Core engineering velocity drops during model development, causing product gap that triggers churn in the existing customer base — eliminating more revenue than the new product projects to generate.
failureModes: A customer discovers their data was used, posts publicly, the story is picked up as a privacy violation — coordinated opt-out campaign, regulatory complaint, and customer churn costs more than the entire projected lifetime revenue of the AI product.

The pilot buyer finds predictions useful in aggregate but unreliable at the individual level, declines to convert, and the company has no second buyer — leaving a production model with ongoing maintenance costs and zero revenue while the core product has 6–12 months of deferred work.

Legal review concludes existing data cannot be used without re-consent, re-consent achieves 15–30% opt-in (typical for non-default consent requests), and the resulting dataset is too small and biased to train a model with generalisable predictive power.

userChallenges: The customers whose data is being used are not the target buyers — they are the raw material. They have no representation in the value chain and receive no benefit from their data being monetised. Research on data trust consistently shows that customers who feel their data was repurposed without meaningful consent express betrayal disproportionate to the actual harm. The relationship damage lands on the core product, not the AI subsidiary.

The Builder's extension to 'conduct a consent audit before building' assumes the audit clears the path. A consent audit for behavioural data collected under a service relationship almost never confirms that third-party commercial AI training is permitted. The audit's most likely output is 'the current policy does not cover this use case' — which means the company must re-consent its entire customer base (low response rate, high opt-out) or abandon the data.
adoptionRisks: Third-party buyers are the customers of the AI product, but no specific problem has been identified that this model solves better than alternatives they already use. Buyers sophisticated enough to purchase enterprise AI inference are also sophisticated enough to ask 'whose data is this, and can I see the consent documentation?' — a question this proposal cannot currently answer.

Even if buyers are interested, the inference API model requires buyers to integrate an API into their own systems, go through a procurement cycle, and rely on reliability guarantees from a company not known as an AI vendor. The company's brand is in its core service category — not AI infrastructure — meaning it starts with no trust capital in the buyer category it is entering.

strengths: The consent audit extension (Builder extension 1) is the only correct first move — it either unlocks the path or stops the idea before sunk costs accumulate.

The inference API reframe (Builder extension 3) is architecturally correct if the idea proceeds: keeping weights proprietary and creating a contractual off-switch is strictly better than selling a trained model.

The opt-in data-contribution programme (Builder non-obvious angle 1) is the cleanest version of this idea — it produces a legally defensible dataset and turns customers into partners rather than subjects.
suggestedPivots: Commission external privacy legal review before any model training begins — the legal basis question is the only gate that matters.
Secure a signed letter of intent or paid pilot agreement from one named third-party company specifying the problem, performance threshold, and price before committing any engineering resources.
If legal review is negative, reframe entirely around a prospective opt-in data programme — smaller dataset, clean consent, customers as stakeholders.
openQuestions: Has the existing privacy policy been reviewed by external privacy counsel against GDPR Article 6 and CCPA for compatibility with secondary commercial AI training?
Who specifically would buy this product, what decision would they use it for, and what are they currently using at what cost to make that decision today?
At what re-consent participation rate does the training dataset become too small to produce reliable signal, and is that rate achievable?
